briefings.title: Synthetic users: explore with them, verify with people
briefings.dek: Teams must decide which research jobs AI can take over and which still need real participants.
briefings.scenario: A research group at a large retailer is told to cut recruitment spend and wants AI-simulated users to pre-screen a checkout redesign. The same group is also considering AI to code thousands of open-ended survey comments and to synthesize interview notes.

positions.label: Divergent thinking, not verdicts
positions.summary: Nielsen sees synthetic users as useful early in design, where they help teams reflect on usage and generate more directions. He also warns that their feedback skews too positive, which weakens them as evidence of how real people will respond.

positions.label: Test the substitution claim
positions.summary: MeasuringU frames the cost and speed appeal of simulated participants as a hypothesis to check, for example by comparing digital-twin predictions of usability scores with real ones. It also revisits AI coding of open-ended comments, a narrower analysis job it thought promising. Product Talk describes AI synthesis of interviews that depends on evaluation and repair loops.

briefings.context: Recruitment is a large and slow part of research budgets, which is why simulated participants are attractive. The sources separate two uses: AI standing in for participants, and AI helping analyze data that real participants produced. The second use keeps people at the source of the evidence.

steps.label: Separate the jobs
steps.text: List which research tasks are idea generation, which are analysis of real data, and which are evidence about real behavior, and only consider AI substitution for the first two.

steps.label: Benchmark against humans
steps.text: Before relying on simulated users or AI coding, run both alongside a real-participant study and compare how closely the results match.

steps.label: Build in checks
steps.text: For AI synthesis, add review steps and error-correction loops, and watch for overly favorable feedback from simulated users.

briefings.caveat: The excerpts do not show the results of the digital-twin score comparison or the ChatGPT coding comparison, so how well AI performs on those tasks remains unsettled here.

briefings.title: Delegating to agents without losing your judgment
briefings.dek: Teams must decide whether skill loss from AI delegation is a real threat to guard against or a worry built on weak evidence.
briefings.scenario: A design team at a large retailer starts running several AI agents at once, one on library updates, one on critique notes, one on spec drafts. Output doubles, but the lead notices that nobody can say how the pieces fit together, and junior designers are making fewer of their own calls.

positions.label: Skill erosion is real
positions.summary: Three pieces argue that handing thinking to AI wears down reasoning, weakens taste, and fragments attention. One author describes producing more than ever while no longer being able to see any project as a whole.

positions.label: Delegation is a skill
positions.summary: Nielsen's roundup claims most deskilling studies examine the wrong condition, which weakens the alarm. Figma's workflow piece treats choosing what to hand to an agent as a skill in itself, with the designer keeping the core shaping work.

briefings.context: Agents now run in parallel on routine design tasks such as library maintenance, feedback synthesis and spec drafting. That raises output but changes where designers spend attention. The debate is about whether the lost practice is the kind that matters: taste, reasoning, and a sense of the whole.

steps.label: Name your core work
steps.text: Decide which decisions, such as framing the problem and judging quality, stay with a human, and hand off only the surrounding tasks.

steps.label: Review as a whole
steps.text: Set aside regular time to look at agent output together as one system, so the overall picture doesn't dissolve into separate deliveries.

steps.label: Keep practice alive
steps.text: Have designers, juniors especially, still do some work unaided and make critique calls before consulting an agent.

briefings.caveat: These are excerpts only, so they don't show what evidence the deskilling studies use or what the 'wrong condition' is, and none of them tests whether any workflow actually preserves judgment.
